emerging_technology: Bidirectional electric-vehicle charging using vehicle-to-grid (V2G) systems.
intended_application: Offer fleet customers a dealership-installed charging service that allows parked electric vehicles to supply electricity to the grid when authorized, while preserving enough charge for scheduled driving.
organization: A hypothetical regional automotive dealership group that sells electric vehicles and earns recurring revenue from vehicle servicing.
business_need: Create a recurring customer service beyond vehicle sales and conventional maintenance.
users_stakeholders: Dealership staff, fleet operators, drivers, and the local electricity utility.
adoption_posture: Innovator — explore a small fleet pilot with a utility and compatible equipment supplier before selling the service widely.
capabilities_constraints: The dealership has vehicle sales and servicing expertise but no established grid-services business. Vehicle compatibility, utility participation, customer contracts, and manufacturer warranty conditions remain unconfirmed.
risk_consequence_context: A vehicle could lack sufficient charge when a customer needs it. Unclear responsibility for battery wear or charging failures could cause disputes and undermine customer trust.
management_question: Could a V2G service give the dealership a viable recurring revenue stream, or would the utility and charging provider capture most of the value while the dealership carries the customer-service burden?
time_horizon: Near- to mid-term: decide whether to run a fleet pilot within 12 months and assess a commercial offering over 24 months.
additional_context: This is a hypothetical breadth-test case, not a claim about an actual dealership or verified deployment. Do not assume all electric vehicles support bidirectional charging, that grid export is permitted, or that customers would earn a profit. Treat those points as evidence needs. Separate technical invention from commercial innovation in the dealership’s offering. Consider the counter-case that installation and support remain ordinary dealership services rather than a new business model. No performance results or source evidence are supplied. This case deliberately changes the technology and industry; it does not test stability of the primary MCP technology classification.
